concern.concern: Proof 2.1 chooses a disk 'of least transverse width modulo the deck translations' without defining that width or establishing attainment, then asserts that intersections with translates produce a smaller-width disk. This is the thin part of the argument that a planar bigon projects injectively to the torus. The standard bigon criterion supplies the intended justification, but the stated minimization needs clarification or an exact external-input citation.

original_concerns.reason: The proposed transverse width is not defined, its minimum is not established, and intersections with translates are not shown to reduce it. Finite interior intersection minimization alone does not justify the claimed injective projection. The exact existing cited surface bigon-lift lemma supplies the missing operation. A meeting pair of periodic lifts has two distinct intersections x and T_v(x), so its contrapositive applies directly; finite bigon removal then preserves the full original isotopy conclusion.

required_own_edits.proposed_replacement:
[A1] Identify $T$ with $\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ so the coordinate loops represent $[\mu]$ and $[\lambda]$; the chosen basis fixes this coordinate convention.

[F1] **External input (bigon lift criterion).** If two transverse simple closed curves on a surface have a pair of lifts to the universal cover intersecting more than once, the curves form an embedded bigon. The innermost-disk construction makes its interior disjoint from the curves. This is the contrapositive of Lemma 1.8, including its embedded projection argument, in Farb–Margalit, *A Primer on Mapping Class Groups*, version 5.0, printed pp.32–33; Proposition 1.7 on p.31 is the bigon criterion. [Farb–Margalit](https://pagine.dm.unipi.it/~a019210/Farb%20Magalit_Primer%20on%20Teichmuller%20theory.pdf)

required_own_edits.source_excerpt: 2.1 Suppose $\gamma_0,\gamma_1$ are essential simple closed curves whose primitive classes agree up to sign. Reverse one orientation if necessary so their classes agree, and isotope them to be transverse. Let $v$ be their common primitive class and let $A=\mathbb R^2/\langle T_v\rangle$ be the cyclic cover of $T$ corresponding to the subgroup generated by $v$. A lift of each curve to $A$ is an embedded essential circle representing the generator of $H_1(A;\mathbb Z)$. Their algebraic intersection in the annulus $A$ is zero, so if they meet the signed crossing count in a fundamental period has both signs. Lift these circles to the universal cover $\mathbb R^2$ of $A$. Their chosen lifts are proper lines invariant under the same translation $T_v$; they have the same two ends at infinity. Opposite-sign crossings on this pair of lines have a bounded complementary disk between subarcs, by the Jordan curve theorem. Among all such disks choose one with the fewest interior intersections with lifted curves, and among ties one of least transverse width modulo the deck translations. Any lifted arc entering its interior cuts off a disk with fewer interior intersections; any nontrivial translate meeting it yields a disk of smaller transverse width. Thus its interior misses every lift and translate, so it projects injectively to an embedded bigon in $T$. Isotoping one curve across this bigon removes exactly two intersections and creates none. Since the original intersection set is finite, repetition terminates and makes the curves disjoint. Cutting $T$ along $\gamma_0$ gives an annulus, and the disjoint essential curve $\gamma_1$ is parallel to its core, so the two curves cobound a subannulus. Isotopy across that annulus carries $\gamma_0$ to $\gamma_1$. Thus the primitive class modulo simultaneous sign determines exactly one unoriented isotopy class. [given, A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct] ∎
required_own_edits.proposed_replacement: 2.1 Suppose $\gamma_0,\gamma_1$ are essential simple closed curves whose primitive classes agree up to sign. Reverse one orientation if necessary so their classes agree, and isotope them to be transverse. Let $v\in\mathbb Z^2$ be their common primitive class in the coordinates of [A1]. If they intersect, choose lifts $\widetilde\gamma_0,\widetilde\gamma_1\subset\mathbb R^2$ through one lift $x$ of an intersection point. Each chosen lift is preserved by the same nonzero deck translation $T_v$, because its projected curve represents $v$. Hence both $x$ and $T_v(x)$ lie on this pair of lifts and are distinct. By [F1] the curves therefore form an embedded bigon in $T$ whose interior misses them. Isotoping one curve across this bigon removes exactly two intersections and creates none. The transverse intersection set is finite, so repetition terminates and makes the curves disjoint. Cutting $T$ along $\gamma_0$ gives an annulus, and the disjoint essential curve $\gamma_1$ is parallel to its core, so the two curves cobound a subannulus. Isotopy across that annulus carries $\gamma_0$ to $\gamma_1$. Thus the primitive class modulo simultaneous sign determines exactly one unoriented isotopy class. [given, A1, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct] ∎
